extracted.intended_audience: students, historians, and practitioners of classical Greek mathematics; mathematicians interested in geometric methods and history of mathematics
extracted.subtask_description: A close reading and use of Archimedes' treatise 'The Method' (with Heath's introduction and editorial notes) describing the mechanical method of discovery and its rigorous geometric supplements for quadrature, cubature, and centres of gravity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between investigation and rigorous proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Archimedes distinguishes between (1) means sufficient to suggest or investigate the truth of theorems (θεωρεῖν) and (2) rigid geometrical demonstrations that actually prove them (ἀποδεικνύναι).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The mechanical method is explicitly said to be useful for discovery and for indicating truths but not sufficient as a final demonstration; a geometrical supplement (usually by the method of exhaustion) must follow to provide an irrefragable proof. Example: Archimedes often 'investigates' by mechanics and then supplies or promises geometric proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanical method: weigh infinitesimal corresponding elements
rubrics_metrics.description: To find area/volume or centre of gravity of a figure X, weigh infinitesimal elements (straight-line strips for plane figures; thin laminae for solids) of X against corresponding elements of a figure B whose area/volume and centre of gravity are known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place X and B so they share the same axis (common diameter) and cut both by parallel planes perpendicular to that axis to obtain corresponding elements. Use the lever (axis extended) and consider moments of elements about the point of suspension to deduce relations between integrals (moments) of X and B. The technique avoids a direct integration for X by reducing to an integral already known for B.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arrange figures with a common axis and use parallel-section elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Figures X and B are positioned so that they have a common straight line (diameter/axis); sections by parallel planes perpendicular to that axis produce corresponding elements whose centres lie on the axis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the elements as 'straight lines' for areas and 'plane areas' for solids (i.e. infinitesimally thin strips/laminae). This ensures the centres of gravity of elements lie on the axis and makes moment calculations feasible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concentrate elements of X at one lever point while leaving B in place
rubrics_metrics.description: Move all corresponding infinitesimal elements of X to a single fixed distance (a) from the fulcrum on the extended axis (so they act at one lever point), while leaving the elements of B at their actual distances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By doing so the moments contributed by all elements of X have the same arm length and sum to (area or volume of X) * a, while the sum of moments of elements of B equals its known centre-of-gravity distance times its area/volume. Equate moments to solve for X's area/volume (or centre of gravity when inverted).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of moments about the fulcrum (lever principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Archimedes computes products of each elemental area/volume by the distance of its centre of gravity from the point of suspension and uses equality of total moments to derive area/volume relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He assumes the principle that the sum of moments of particles or elements acting at their actual places equals the moment of the whole applied at its centre of gravity. Algebraically represented in the text by integrals such as ∫ u·x dx etc., and by proportional moment equations like (area of X)·a = (area of B)·b.

rubrics_metrics.name: Breadth/thickness cancels; treatment of infinitesimal elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Elements are conceived as indefinitely narrow strips (areas) or indefinitely thin laminae (solids); their common infinitesimal breadth or thickness cancels out of moment ratios and so need not be included explicitly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Archimedes does not explicitly invoke a formal limiting/integral notion; he treats the number of elements as infinite implicitly and relies on the cancellative property of the uniform small thickness when comparing corresponding elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prerequisite knowledge of centres of gravity and volumes of standard solids
rubrics_metrics.description: The method presupposes known facts: centre of gravity of a straight line is its midpoint; of a triangle is intersection of medians; of a parallelogram is intersection of diagonals; centre of a circle is its centre; centre of a cylinder is midpoint of axis; centre of a cone divides axis in ratio 3:1 (vertex portion triple base portion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These propositions (listed in the preface) are used as basic, previously proved facts when applying the mechanical method; they are required ingredients to compute moments and deduce unknown areas/volumes/centres.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduce unknowns to known integrals via auxiliary figures
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce auxiliary figures B (and possibly C) with known area/volume/centre so that corresponding-section integrals of the unknown figure X can be equated to (or combined with) known integrals of B to solve for X.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include weighing X alone against B, or weighing X+V against B, yielding linear relations like (X + V)·a = B·b. Choice of B is strategic: standard solids (triangles, cones, cylinders, spheres) are typical choices because their moments are known.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method-of-exhaustion supplement for rigorous proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the mechanical method gives an investigation and persuasive demonstration, Archimedes uses the method of exhaustion (inscribing/circumscribing approximating solids and taking limits) to produce the rigorous geometric proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For final acceptance Archimedes constructs inscribed and circumscribed element-prisms/rectangles and shows their difference can be made arbitrarily small, thereby proving equalities of areas/volumes in the limit. This is the standard way he converts mechanical insights into rigorous results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of symmetry, axis extension, and lever geometry to position centres
rubrics_metrics.description: Extend axes (produce lines to points H etc.), use symmetry or special points (midpoints, centres) to set up levers and to compute distances of centres of gravity for moment equations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical device: extend an axis to a point H such that HA equals a specified length (e.g. HA = AC) and regard the extended axis segment (e.g. CH or HC) as the bar of a balance, choosing its midpoint and other division points to locate centres of gravity algebraically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance corresponding cross-sections across different solids
rubrics_metrics.description: For many propositions, show that for every plane cutting solids in corresponding circles/lines, the section from one solid placed at its centre balances the corresponding sections from other solids placed at a designated point; integrating these balances over all sections yields relationships between whole solids.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This technique is used repeatedly (sphere vs cone vs cylinder, spheroid vs cone vs cylinder, paraboloid vs cone vs cylinder, etc.). The local (section-wise) equilibrium implies global volumetric ratios after summing/integrating over the family of sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use auxiliary curves (parabola) to reduce cubature to known quadrature
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce auxiliary planar curves (e.g. a parabola) to analytically reduce a 3D cubature problem to a 2D quadrature problem already solved, enabling the use of previous quadrature results to handle volumes bounded by planes and curved surfaces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In propositions concerning portions of cylinders cut by oblique planes, Archimedes uses an auxiliary parabola so that ratios of element-prisms correspond to ratios of element-rectangles for which quadrature is known (Quadrature of the Parabola). This is an example of transforming a difficult solid problem into a simpler planar one.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inscribe/circumscribe element-prisms and use limiting arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove equalities of solids, inscribe and circumscribe solids made up of element-prisms (whose bases are small planar figures) so that the circumscribed exceeds the inscribed by an arbitrarily small amount; then use proportionality of corresponding elements to derive contradictions if equality failed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The construction: divide an axis into many small equal parts, draw planes through division points to produce element-prisms; compare sums of element-prisms between figures and exploit known proportionalities (e.g. MN^2 : MO^2) to carry the exhaustion argument. This is the geometric basis for strict proofs following mechanical suggestion.

rubrics_metrics.name: List of worked theorem-targets as methodological exemplars
rubrics_metrics.description: Archimedes applies the mechanical method to concrete targets (examples): segment of a parabola is 4/3 of corresponding triangle; sphere is 4 times the cone with base a great circle and height equal to the radius; cylinder relations with sphere and cone; paraboloid segment = 3× cone; portions of cylinders related to prisms, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These worked examples serve both as demonstrations of the mechanical method and as templates for applying the method to other quadrature/cubature problems. Each example shows choice of auxiliary solid(s), axis placement, section correspondence, moment equations, and geometric supplements.
